context: Current closing price of Sherwin-Williams (SHW): $366.55 USD as of 2026-08-05.
justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assessed as the current price level near $367–368 for this asset (which appears to be in the neighborhood of a broad equity index or ETF). At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price, expecting mean-reversion dynamics to dominate over such a short window with only a small positive drift assumption baked in. At the one-week horizon, I allowed for slightly more upward movement, reflecting a mild bullish baseline consistent with long-run equity risk premium assumptions and assuming no major macro surprises materialize. At the one-month horizon, the drift becomes slightly more pronounced, as compounding over roughly 20 trading days gives more room for the underlying trend to express itself, while still remaining close to current levels given the uncertainty involved.

The confidence interval widths grow systematically with time, which reflects the square-root-of-time scaling of volatility that is foundational to most asset price models. At one day, realized volatility in equity markets typically implies a daily move of roughly 1–1.5%, so a 90% confidence interval spanning about $19 wide is consistent with that. As we extend to one week and one month, the uncertainty fans out considerably, with the one-month interval spanning roughly $68, reflecting that markets can absorb significant new information over that period. I also gave some weight to the possibility of elevated near-term volatility given macro conditions, which widened the intervals slightly relative to a pure historical-volatility assumption.

Specific tail risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include a sudden shift in Federal Reserve policy signaling — either a surprise hawkish pivot or unexpected rate cuts — which has historically caused outsized single-day moves in equity indices. Geopolitical escalation, a credit event in a systemically important institution, or a significant earnings miss from a heavily weighted index constituent could all produce moves exceeding my stated bounds. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected economic data release or a de-escalation of trade or geopolitical tensions could generate a sharp rally beyond the upper bound of my one-month interval.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume roughly log-normal return distributions, which historically underweight extreme events. Fat tails in actual equity returns mean that moves beyond two standard deviations occur more frequently than a Gaussian model would suggest, so my stated 90% confidence intervals should be understood as somewhat optimistic in their coverage — real-world outcomes will escape these bounds more than 10% of the time over a long sample of comparable forecasts.
